name: Wristmogging

lead: Wristmogging is looksmaxxing slang for out-sizing another person's wrists. 'Mogging' means outshining someone in appearance, and the term traces to the acronym AMOG, for 'alpha male of the group' [1].

The wrist is used as a quick marker of frame width: thick wrists are read as part of a broad, sturdy skeleton that makes shoulders and forearms look larger. The wrist consists of eight carpal bones plus the ends of the radius and ulna [2].

paras: In practice it is a comparison made visually or by wrapping fingers around the wrist, often shown in photos with watches or hands side by side. People who want to look more imposing work on forearm and overall muscle, which can make wrists look thicker in proportion.
There are no health risks specific to the concept. Wrist circumference is mostly set by bone structure and cannot be changed much by training.

angle.text: People comparing wrists treat thick wrists as part of what makes a frame look wide. Since bone width is largely fixed, people who want a bigger-looking wrist-and-forearm area focus on building the muscle around it.

lead: Wristmogging is a term from looksmaxxing culture for having larger wrists than another person, framed as evidence of a wider skeletal frame. 'Mogging' is slang for outshining others, usually in looks or status, and derives from the acronym AMOG, meaning 'alpha male of the group', which dates to manosphere communities of the early 2000s before becoming a verb in the 2010s [1].

The wrist is a convenient frame marker because it is bony and visible. It contains eight carpal bones in two rows, joined to the radius, ulna and the five metacarpals [2]. Communities treat wrist circumference as a proxy for frame width alongside shoulder and clavicle breadth, and a thicker wrist is considered to add to a masculine, powerful look.
No published study has tested wrist thickness as a factor in perceived attractiveness.

paras: Wristmogging combines 'wrist' with 'mogging'. Linguists trace mogging to the acronym AMOG, which appeared in early-2000s manosphere communities, and by the 2010s it was the verb 'mog' with a meaning shifted toward physical superiority [1].
The wrist's bony structure comprises eight carpal bones in a proximal and distal row, with the distal radius and ulna on the forearm side [2].
